synopsis: A rainy night commute climbs out of the city, crosses a luminous spore layer and arrives on a bioluminescent moon under an enormous gas giant.

shots.prompt:
HOOK. Open already mid-motion on one ordinary object passing the glass at arm's length, so close and so fast it is only a streak. A dull, grey, utterly routine commute. At 1.5 seconds a two-note chime cuts in and a calm neutral announcer says the destination line. Nobody reacts and nothing changes. The train immediately accelerates hard. By 6 seconds ONE thing far ahead is unmistakably wrong, and it is already growing.

A rainy night commute through wet city outskirts. A petrol station canopy post whips past the glass close enough to blur, neon signs and bus shelters stripping backward, tower blocks stacked behind, rain streaking the outside of the window. The announcer says exactly: "Next stop: Aloran." The train slams into acceleration. By 6 seconds the line has begun to climb and the street lights are already dropping below the level of the track.

HARD BREACH. In the first half second something enormous slams past the glass at arm's length and blacks the frame out for an instant. Coming out of that darkness the ordinary world is already gone and the line has physically committed to the destination with no way back. The shot ends with the destination's first true landmark resolving far ahead.

The carriage judders hard as a viaduct pier slams past the glass and blacks the frame. The line is now climbing steeply and the bodies press back. The city becomes a grid of orange lights far below, shrinking; the rain stops hitting the glass; the horizon takes a visible curve and the sky drains from sodium orange through deep blue toward black as the last cloud deck falls away beneath the window.

ARRIVAL EDGE. Open on a violent change of light in the first half second: the exposure blows out white or crushes to black and recovers. Then the first landmark grows continuously across the whole shot until it no longer fits inside the window. Show how far down or how far up the place goes. The scale must be frightening.

A violent jolt shakes the camera as the train punches through the last haze band of atmosphere. The sky is now black and full of hard unblinking stars. Earth fills the lower half of the window as a lit curved sphere, continent lights and terminator visible, and it is measurably shrinking. The carriage interior is lit only by its own strip lights against that black.

FLYTHROUGH. Open with that landmark's mass already passing the window at close range, filling the glass and strobing the interior. Maximum parallax: foreground elements cross the frame in a fraction of a second while the true size of the place is revealed by what lies beyond them. Something larger still is already visible ahead.

The carriage judders. Earth has become a bright blue dot receding among the stars behind, and the star field streams past the window with real parallax: near stars whipping across the frame in an instant, far ones barely moving. A dust ribbon passes close and blacks out part of the view. Far ahead a banded gas giant already hangs, growing, with one small moon crossing its face.

DEEPEST SCALE. Open with a hard impact against the glass in the first half second - heat, pressure, spray or a shockwave that jolts the camera and knocks the focus. Then the widest and deepest view of the destination so far, too large for the window to contain. The single most spectacular second of the episode belongs here.

THE IMPACT: the train slams into the moon's upper atmosphere. The whole carriage shakes hard enough to blur the frame, the pole rattles, plasma glare rips white-orange along the glass and streams backward past the window. Deceleration presses everything forward. Through the fire the first ground is visible far below: a luminous blue-green forest floor and an unbroken cloud ocean, rising fast.

HEART AND PAYOFF. Open with the train passing through or beneath something colossal. Travel alone carries it into the centre of the place. At about 8.5 seconds a calm ordinary commuter announcer quietly says the arrival line. Then the chime sounds again, the same voice begins only "Next stop-" and the shot ends mid-word while the train is still moving forward and something new is already growing ahead.

A last hard jolt and the plasma tears away. The train levels out into alien night beneath the gas giant, which now fills a third of the sky and lights the ground. It passes beneath a root arch so vast its underside fills the entire window, then into the heart of the place: a tree organism kilometres tall, bioluminescent settlements glowing on suspended platforms among its branches, spore drifts rising past the glass. The sky overhead is deep black. The announcer says exactly: "Welcome to Aloran."
